content:
Saskatchewan residents will have another opportunity to watch for shooting stars this November as the annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak around Nov. 17-18.

Known for their exceptionally fast-moving meteors, the Leonids are among the more recognizable annual meteor showers.

Although they do not always produce large numbers of shooting stars, their speed and occasional spectacular displays make them worth watching.

Comet debris creates the display

The Leonids originate from debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.

As Earth passes through the comet's debris stream, small particles enter the atmosphere at high speeds, producing the bright streaks of light visible from the ground.

Leonid meteors travel at approximately 70 kilometres per second.

The shower gets its name from the constellation Leo, where its radiant appears to be located.

However, observers do not need to stare directly at Leo. Meteors can appear across the entire sky.

A history of spectacular displays

The Leonids have a particularly interesting history.

In certain years, the shower has produced spectacular meteor storms, with thousands of meteors appearing within a relatively short period.

Those displays are uncommon and are associated with Earth passing through particularly dense concentrations of cometary debris.

For 2026, observers should expect a more modest display, with approximately 10 to 15 meteors per hour possible under ideal conditions.

The first-quarter Moon will set around midnight, helping provide darker conditions during the later part of the night.

When and where to watch

The best viewing opportunities are generally after midnight and before dawn, when the constellation Leo is higher in the sky.

The first-quarter Moon will set around midnight, allowing for darker conditions during the later hours of the night.

Find a dark location away from artificial lighting and give your eyes time to adjust.

No telescope or binoculars are necessary, as the unaided eye provides the widest view of the sky.

Taking in the night sky

Abigail Sadowski of Kalium Observatory, affiliated with the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada, also highlighted the importance of taking in the entire night sky.

"These are so huge. They take up such a huge portion of the sky that they're best observed with the naked eye," she said.

Preparing for a night outdoors

Sadowski says winter can actually offer some advantages for observing.

"Typically, we like to observe in the winter when the air is a little bit steadier and we get typically less cloud rainstorms," she said.

However, November temperatures can make extended outdoor observing challenging.

Sadowski offered a simple reminder for anyone planning to spend time outside.

"Please dress warmly," she said.
